source.title_on_document: Exploring the Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Creative Thinking Processes: results from a preliminary study.

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is identified in the saved PDF. Results are in the main text (pp. 6-8); the document ends with references (pp. 11-12).

paper_design_summary: University students were explicitly described as randomly assigned to use generative AI for preparatory text-analysis/evaluation questions or to complete the activity without digital support, although the authors also call the design quasi-experimental (p. 3, Section 2.1). Both groups then produced a social media post scored with a creative-production rubric; AI permission was restricted to the preceding questions, so the outcome answers after_ai (pp. 3-6, Sections 2.1-2.3). In total, 56 students were analyzed, 28 per arm; coursework recruitment is stated, but the activity setting needed to distinguish field, lab, or online RCT is not established (p. 4, Section 2.2; p. 6, Table 1).

studies.label: AI-supported text analysis followed by an unaided creative social media post

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students to an experimental group allowed AI tools for the first two Analysis/Evaluation questions, or a control group completing the entire activity without digital support. Random assignment is explicitly stated despite the quasi-experimental label. The assignment method and sequence generation are not described.
assignment.quote: The sample, composed of university students, was randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: p. 3, section 2.1 (Research Design). Conflicting quasi-experimental characterization: p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, section 2.1; pp. 9–10, section 5.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is reported in the saved PDF (pp. 1-12).

arms.name: Group A – with AI
arms.description: Allowed generative AI tools when answering the preparatory Analysis/Evaluation questions; this permission did not extend to the final Creation question (p. 3, section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract). The analyzed count is the N printed for creative performance in p. 6, Table 1.

arms.name: Group B – without digital tools
arms.description: Completed the entire activity without any digital support (p. 3, section 2.1). The analyzed count is the N printed for creative performance in p. 6, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition flow are reported. The authors explicitly retained one Management Engineering Master’s student in the analyses (p. 4, section 2.2). Assignment-stage counts are not separately given, so n_randomized is left null; the group counts are taken from the outcome analysis (p. 6, Table 1).
participants.who: Convenience sample of university students recruited during regular coursework, mainly in Economics and Data Analysis or Business Economics. The sample is described as undergraduate, but the authors also state that one Management Engineering Master’s student was included and retained (p. 4, section 2.2).
participants.quote: The sample consisted of 56 undergraduate students, evenly distributed by gender, with a mean age of 21 years; approximately 80% of the participants were aged 21 or younger.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 2.2 (Sample); p. 6, Table 1 (28 analyzed in each arm); p. 1, Abstract (fifty-six students completed the creative task).

ai_tool.how_used: Unspecified generative AI tools were permitted for the two Analysis/Evaluation questions about the reading, preceding the creative post (p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 2.1). The role is analytical reading support. The provider, model, interface, prompts, amount of use, exposure duration, and compliance checks are not reported. Interaction quality was not directly observed or standardized (p. 9, Section 4). PsyToolkit and/or Google Forms are questionnaire platforms, not identified AI interventions (p. 4, Section 2.3).

task.description: Read Matteo Minelli’s text “Tribal Economy: When Not Doing Becomes Abundance,” answer the preparatory analysis/evaluation questions, and then create a post for Instagram, X/Twitter or Facebook. The post could contain up to 800 characters, including a title/slogan, and had to creatively synthesize and reinterpret the ideas of an economy of abundance and not doing in contemporary society (pp. 3–5, sections 2.1 and 2.3).

outcomes.name: Total_Create: total creative production rubric score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An analytic rubric scored the social media post on conceptual re-elaboration, originality and synthesis of the message, thematic relevance, and linguistic appropriateness and communicative tone. Each indicator was rated 0–3, for a maximum total of 12 points (pp. 5-6, Section 2.3). The document does not identify who or what applied the rubric, assessor expertise or number, blinding, or reliability; the measure category is therefore null. Total_Create is the only rubric outcome with a reported group comparison (p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2). No explicit primary-outcome designation is stated. The analysis reports a score for each participant, who produced one post.
outcomes.delay: The post follows the analytical questions in the same described activity; no elapsed time or later-session delay is stated (pp. 3-4, Section 2.1).

contrasts.reported: Analyzed creative-performance sample: Group A – with AI: N = 28, Mean = 8.21, Std. Dev. = 1.97; Group B – without digital tools: N = 28, Mean = 7.64, Std. Dev. = 1.94. The text reports +0.57 points, p = .31, and Cohen’s d = 0.26. No standard error, confidence interval, test statistic, or degrees of freedom are reported for this contrast. All values are transcribed as printed; no effect size or standard error has been computed.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2 (Creative Performance Results); interpretation continues on p. 7.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria on the saved paper. Section 2.1 explicitly states random assignment of individual university students to generative-AI permission for preparatory analysis/evaluation or no digital support (p. 3; GenAI identified in the p. 1 Abstract). Table 1 reports 28 analyzed students per arm, consistent with the 56-person sample in Section 2.2 (pp. 4 and 6). The rubric scores the creative post itself, including originality (pp. 5-6, Section 2.3). AI permission is restricted to the preparatory questions, supporting after_ai for the subsequent post under the stated protocol (pp. 3-4, Section 2.1). The conflicting quasi-experimental label and causal-inference caveat remain an eligibility-relevant clarification for the authors (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9-10, Section 5); they do not override the explicit random-assignment statement in this screening. Unknown scorer identity and task setting do not negate output scoring or random assignment; measure and design_class remain null. Table 2 concerns A.S.K. performance bands and does not revise the creative-post analysis counts (p. 7).

one_line_finding: Among 56 students analyzed, those allowed AI during the preceding analysis scored 8.21 (SD 1.97, n = 28) versus 7.64 (SD 1.94, n = 28) on the subsequent unaided creative post, with no statistically significant difference (p = .31; printed Cohen’s d = 0.26; p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2).
open_questions: Who or what applied the creative-production rubric? Assessor type, expertise, number, blinding, and reliability are unspecified, so the measure category remains null for the total and components (pp. 5-6, Section 2.3).

Was the creative activity conducted within ordinary coursework, in a separate supervised research session, or remotely? Coursework recruitment and online questionnaire collection do not establish the task setting, so the agreed field_rct code could not be confirmed (p. 4, Sections 2.2-2.3).

How was random assignment implemented, and why is the study also described as quasi-experimental? The randomization field follows the explicit procedural statement, while the terminology conflict is retained (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9-10, Section 5).

Which generative AI tool/model was used, how much was it used, and how was restriction to the analytical questions enforced? The after_ai code follows the stated protocol, not verified access logs (p. 3, Section 2.1; p. 9, Section 4).

When was A.S.K. administered relative to AI exposure, and how should the inconsistent gender counts be interpreted? Table 2 prints Male n = 20, Female n = 15, and Total n = 37 in the Average row (p. 7); this table is not used to change the creative-post analysis count.
notes: Reconciled both valid raw forms after reading all 365 markdown lines and extracting all 12 PDF pages, including references; no appendix is present. All retained numerical findings were checked against PDF text, with text-strategy table extraction additionally checked for Tables 1 and 2. No effect sizes or standard errors were calculated. The journal header and copyright show 2026, while filenames and the candidate record use 2025 (p. 1). The assignment-stage sample count, participant country, task duration, AI model, preregistration, supplement, sample reuse, and study data/code URLs are not stated. Random assignment is coded from the explicit procedural statement; the conflicting quasi-experimental terminology is preserved (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9-10, Section 5). The design subtype is null because recruitment during coursework does not establish whether the task occurred within coursework, in a lab, or remotely (p. 4). Immediate timing and after_ai follow the stated task sequence and restriction of AI permission, without a stated numeric delay or documented compliance procedure (pp. 3-4). The total and four separately rated rubric components are retained; only the total has a reported arm comparison, and the scorer category is unknown (pp. 5-6). A.S.K. creative-potential scores are reported by performance band and gender, with no AI-condition comparison or stated administration timing relative to AI exposure (p. 5, Section 2.3; p. 7, Section 3.3 and Table 2). Table 2 prints below-average n = 9 (16.07%), average n = 37 (66.07%), and above-average n = 10 (17.86%). Its Average row has inconsistent gender and total counts; values are preserved as printed, not corrected. DIGCOMP familiarity is self-reported, not a creative-output score (pp. 5-6, Sections 2.3 and 3.1). Correlations with the same creative-post total are overall AI familiarity r = .46, p < .001; Digital content creation r = .51, p < .001; Problem solving r = .48, p < .001; Information and data literacy r = .34, p < .01; Communication and collaboration r = .31, p < .01; and Safety r = .29, p < .05 (p. 8, Section 3.4). The A.S.K. correlation is r = .42, p < .01 (p. 8, Section 3.5). These descriptive distributions and correlations are retained in notes, not as additional AI-condition effects. No comprehension-question accuracy results or across-person diversity measure is reported. Differences count substantive omissions of numerical findings as well as disagreements about outcome inclusion and measurement; wording, encoding, equivalent unknown-value representations, and redundant locators are not counted. n_unresolved counts unresolved differences plus agreed fields that failed source confirmation: the scorer category and the setting-specific design code. Other reporting limitations are documented in open_questions and are not additional screener disagreements. Final review independently covered all 365 markdown lines and all 12 PDF pages, including references; no appendix is present. Tables 1 and 2 were checked with PDF text and table extraction. The assignment, people, and outcome challenge files each contain no problems, so challenge_resolution is empty and all three challenge-resolution counts are zero. The final open_items classify every existing open question, the unresolved scorer difference, and the unconfirmed setting-specific design code. The original reconciliation object is preserved unchanged. Source supplement reporting remains not_stated. This paper reports its own experiment, so the reanalysis design-class rule does not apply. All printed statistics are retained without recalculating effects or uncertainty.

open_items.item: Rubric assessor identity, expertise, number, blinding, and reliability remain unspecified (open_questions[0]; reconciliation.differences[0]). Authors would need to describe who or what applied the rubric. This does not change criterion 3: the paper explicitly scores the produced post, and either human or computed scoring can qualify (pp. 5-6, Section 2.3).

Task administration setting remains unknown (open_questions[1]; unconfirmed studies[0].design_class in reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked). Authors would need to establish whether the activity occurred in ordinary coursework, a supervised research session, or remotely. This determines the RCT subtype, not any eligibility criterion; coursework recruitment and online questionnaire collection alone do not settle it (p. 4, Sections 2.2-2.3).

Random-assignment implementation and the conflicting quasi-experimental characterization remain unexplained (open_questions[2]). Authors would need to confirm the allocation procedure and reconcile the design terminology. This concerns criterion 1 and could change classification if allocation was nonrandom; the current met decision follows the explicit random-assignment statement (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9-10, Section 5).

The generative-AI provider/model, amount of use, and enforcement of the restriction to preparatory analysis remain unreported (open_questions[3]). Authors would need to supply the intervention details and explain access controls or compliance monitoring. GenAI assistance is explicit, so model and dose details do not change criterion 1; access during the final post would affect after_ai versus with_ai coding, both of which can be core-eligible (p. 1, Abstract; pp. 3-4, Section 2.1; p. 9, Section 4).

A.S.K. administration timing relative to AI exposure is not stated (timing portion of open_questions[4]). Authors would need to clarify the task sequence and whether any A.S.K. results compare assigned AI conditions. This could establish an additional eligible outcome but does not change criterion 3, already met by the scored creative post (p. 5, Section 2.3; p. 7, Section 3.3; p. 8, Section 3.5).

The A.S.K. Table 2 gender counts are inconsistent with its total column (count portion of open_questions[4]): the Average row prints male n = 20, female n = 15, and total n = 37. Authors would need to provide corrected counts or explain missing observations. This does not change criterion 2 because the separate creative-post comparison explicitly analyzes 28 students per arm and the sample section reports 56 students (p. 7, Table 2; p. 6, Table 1; p. 4, Section 2.2).
